title: Inheritance, lived
hookLine: dividing an estate by the shares, with fairness and peace

lines: A TABLE, A FOLDER, A FAMILY.
cards: Who gets what? After a funeral, that question can arrive at the kitchen table along with a folder of papers, a cousin who flew in, and tea nobody drinks. Old hurts can come up with it.
Who did more. Who was favored. And sometimes the person who used to settle things is the one who is gone.
The Qur'an walks straight into that room. It doesn't leave the dividing to whoever argues hardest. It names the shares itself.

teach.h: A SHARE FOR MEN, A SHARE FOR WOMEN.
teach.b: Surah al-Nisa opens the subject with a principle, in paraphrase: men have a share of what parents and near relatives leave, and women have a share of what parents and near relatives leave, whether it's little or much, a share that's fixed.
Women named in the same sentence as men. The verses that follow set out the shares in detail: children, parents, spouses, brothers and sisters, each with a portion.
And they end by calling these the limits set by God. So the hardest question at that table is already answered. Nobody has to win the argument.
But a verse just before the detailed shares makes this lived, not just calculated.

teach.h: GIVE TO THOSE PRESENT, AND SPEAK KINDLY.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "And when kinsfolk and orphans and the needy are present at the division (of the heritage), bestow on them therefrom and speak kindly unto them."
Look who's in the room: relatives with no fixed share, an orphan, someone poor standing at the edge. Give them something, and speak kindly. The math is exact.
The manners around it are generous.

Now the week: tears the Prophet called mercy, graves that remind, a greeting that calls them dwellings, three things that continue, charity that still reaches, a will written before the second night, and now the shares, divided with fairness and kind words.
Each is a way the living keep faith with the dead, and with each other, after the funeral is over.

how: Muslims divide an estate according to the shares set out in surah al-Nisa, after debts and any bequest are settled, and Qur'an 4:8 asks that relatives without a share, orphans and the needy who are present be given something and spoken to kindly.

o: a gift to charity of all that a person leaves behind
the shares the Qur'an sets for heirs, given with kindness
whatever the eldest son decides to give each relative

p: a share, in the same sentence

s: the Qur'an leaves the dividing of an estate to the family to argue out
surah al-Nisa names the shares itself.
in the Qur'an, women inherit a share too
men have a share and women have a share, whether little or much.
only the heirs with fixed shares are mentioned at the division
the verse names kinsfolk, orphans and the needy who are present.

games.q: the estate is being divided. a cousin with no share, an orphan and a poor neighbor are in the room. what do you do?
o: ask them to leave; it's family business.
give them something, and speak kindly.
give them nothing, but be polite.
games.why: surah al-Nisa says: bestow on them therefrom and speak kindly unto them.

practice: Bring to mind your own family, or one you know well, and notice any old question of who got what, or who was favored, that still sits between people; you don't have to solve it.
Then think of the verse's two parts, the share that's due and the kind word, and ask where a kind word could go, even if nothing else changes. If you pray, you can remember that family with care.

wordCard.voice: Inheritance. The shares the Qur'an sets for heirs in surah al-Nisa, divided with fairness, with something for those present, and with kind words. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: inheritance, what is passed on.

carryVoice: Your line: shares with peace. A share that's due, and a kind word with it. That's the week.
